question: Which of the following statements regarding fornix-based versus limbal-based trabeculectomies is true?

options.A: the limbal-based approach is associated with a higher rate of wound leaks compared to the fornix-based approach
options.B: the fornix-based approach is technically more difficult compared to the limbal-based approach
options.C: the limbal-based approach has a greater chance of producing a diffuse low bleb compared to a fornix-based approach
options.D: the fornix-based approach promotes filtration of fluid more posteriorly compared to the limbal-based approach

explanation: In fornix-based trabeculectomies, the initial conjunctival incision is actually made at the limbus (yes, this terminology typically confuses new residents being first exposed to filtering surgery). Due to better exposure at the limbus, the fornix-based approach is technically easier and can be done easily without an assistant. In contrast, for limbal-based filters, the conjunctival incision is made 8-10 mm posterior to the limbus (i.e. in the fornix) which is technically more difficult due to poorer exposure. There is a greater incidence of wound leaks in fornix-based filters since the edge of the wound is at the limbus. However, fornix-based filters are thought to produce lower, more diffuse blebs since the subconjunctival scar (created by the suture line) is anterior to the scleral flap. This promotes fluid flow posterior to the flap resulting in a lower, more diffuse filtering bleb. In contrast, the scar in limbal-based filters is posterior to the scleral flap -- therefore, these blebs are typically more focal and elevated. The advantage of limbal-based filters is that wound closure is less prone to leaks since the suture line is far from the limbus. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

question: Most important risk factor for the development and progression of diabetic retinopathy?
explanation: Important long-term data on disease rates and progression, including a direct association between longer duration of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and increased prevalence of diabetic retinopathy, were provided by the WESDR (Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy) Among WESDR participants with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus, nearly 99% of those with type 1 disease and 60% of those with type 2 disease had some degree of diabetic retinopathy. PDR was also reported in 50% of patients with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes and in 25% of those with a 25- year history of type 2 diabetes. In addition, a visual acuity of 20/200 or worse was observed in 3.6% of patients with younger-onset disease (ie, aged <30 years at diagnosis) and 1.6% of patients with older-onset disease (ie, aged 30 years or older at diagnosis). This vision loss was attributed to diabetic retinopathy in 86% of the younger- onset group and 33% of the older-onset group. AAO retina

question: A 75-year-old woman is referred to you by the emergency room for "painless loss of vision" in the left eye. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 and 20/40 in the right and left eyes respectively. There is a brisk afferent pupillary defect in the left eye. Your exam is significant for the findings seen above. A fluorescein angiogram (FA) is performed (frame at 25 seconds shown above). The blood supply preserving this woman's central acuity is a branch most directly from which artery? (same exact Pic)
explanation: C The fundus photo shows retinal whitening but with preservation of perfusion in the foveal area. The corresponding FA shows absence of dye in the majority of the retinal blood vessels except for a few vessels feeding the fovea. This presentation is consistent with a cilioretinal-sparing central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The blood supply to the inner layers of the retina is typically derived entirely from the central retinal artery (CRA). The exception is that approximately 1530% of eyes have a cilioretinal artery which is a branch most directly from the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs). The CRA, PCAs, and lacrimal artery are branches of the ophthalmic artery. Most cases of CRAO are visually-devastating with greater than two-thirds of cases having visual acuity of worse than 20/400. The majority of CRAO cases associated with good central visual acuity are those with a patent cilioretinal artery. Vision of NLP typically does not occur in CRAO, but can occur with simultaneous choroidal infarction (e.g. ophthalmic artery occlusion). 50. question: Mechanism of TAO:
explanation: the presumed mechanism is activation of orbital fibroblasts by Graves' disease-related autoantibodies, which lead to the release of T cell chemoattractants, initiating an interaction which ultimately results in fibroblasts expressing extracellular matrix molecules, biologic materials proliferating and differentiating into myofibroblasts or lipofibroblasts and deposition of glycosaminoglycans which bind water that lead to swelling, congestion in addition to connective tissue remodeling. This results in extraocular muscle enlargement and orbital fat expansion. Reference: https://eyewiki.org/Thyroid_Eye_Disease 74. Obese, difficulty sleeping with conj irritation in the morning?

question: A 71-year-old man presents with concerns about a mass which appeared about 6 months ago, and has slowly enlarged to the point that it now protrudes between his lids. As shown in the photo, exam finds a glistening yellow mass which is painless, soft, and mobile beneath the conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (Exact Picture)
explanation: This newly-developed, soft, glistening, yellow, mobile sub-conjunctival mass is prolapsed orbital fat. In contrast, lipodermoid (aka dermolipoma) (choice "A") is a congenital choristoma comprised of dense fibroconnective tissue and fat, which would have been present since birth, rather than appearing at age 71. Lipodermoids are occasionally associated with oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia (i.e. Goldenhar syndrome). Hemangiopericytoma (choice "B") would be a firm mass, usually located in the retrobulbar intraconal space. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice "D") of the orbit forms a firm mass arising from the lacrimal gland, often causing the appearance of superotemporal lid fullness or non-axial proptosis rather than a sub-conjunctival mass.
